questions.stem: What defines a problem as being in the class P?

options.text: It can be solved in polynomial time.
It can be verified in polynomial time.
It cannot be solved or verified in polynomial time.
It can be solved in exponential time.

questions.explanation: A problem is in the class P if it can be solved by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time. This means that there exists an algorithm that can find a solution to the problem in a time that is a polynomial function of the size of the input. The option stating that it can be verified in polynomial time is tempting, but verification in polynomial time is a characteristic of NP, not P.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of NP problems?

options.text: They can be solved in polynomial time.
They can be verified in polynomial time.
They cannot be verified in polynomial time.
They can only be solved in exponential time.

questions.explanation: NP problems are characterized by the fact that their solutions can be verified in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine. This means that if a solution is given, it can be checked for correctness efficiently. The option suggesting they can be solved in polynomial time is incorrect because not all NP problems are known to be solvable in polynomial time.

questions.stem: What is the complexity class of problems that can be solved by a nondeterministic Turing machine in polynomial time?

options.text: P
NP
EXP
PSPACE

questions.explanation: The complexity class NP consists of problems that can be solved by a nondeterministic Turing machine in polynomial time. This means that a nondeterministic machine can guess a solution and verify its correctness in polynomial time. The other options refer to different complexity classes that do not match this definition.

questions.stem: If a problem is in P, what can be said about its membership in NP?

options.text: It is definitely not in NP.
It is also in NP.
It is in NP only if it is exponential.
It cannot be verified in polynomial time.

questions.explanation: If a problem is in P, it can be solved in polynomial time, which implies that it can also be verified in polynomial time. Therefore, every problem in P is also in NP, as NP includes problems that can be verified in polynomial time. The other options incorrectly suggest restrictions or conditions that do not apply to problems in P.

questions.stem: Explain why proving P = NP or P ≠ NP would have significant implications for fields such as cryptography.
markingGuide: P = NP implies efficient solutions for all verifiable problems.
Cryptographic systems rely on certain problems being hard to solve.
If P = NP, many cryptographic systems could be broken.
P ≠ NP would confirm the security assumptions of cryptography.
questions.explanation: Proving P = NP would imply that problems assumed to be hard (like factoring) could be solved efficiently, threatening cryptographic security. P ≠ NP would support current security assumptions.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding the relationship between P and NP?

options.text: P is a subset of NP.
NP is a subset of P.
P and NP are disjoint sets.
P and NP are identical sets.

questions.explanation: The relationship between P and NP is that P is a subset of NP. This is because any problem that can be solved in polynomial time (P) can also have its solution verified in polynomial time (NP). The other options incorrectly describe the relationship between these classes, as it is not known whether P equals NP or if they are disjoint.
